subject: anatomy
title: Large Intestine: Taeniae Coli, Mesenteric Arteries, and Watershed Zones

steps.tx: The large intestine extends 1.5 meters from the caecum to the anal canal. It is distinguished externally from the small intestine by three unique anatomical cardinal features: longitudinal bands termed taeniae coli, fatty peritoneal pouches termed appendices epiploicae, and sacculations termed **haustrations**.
steps.say: The large intestine extends one and a half meters from caecum to anus. It is distinguished from small bowel by three cardinal features: taeniae coli, fatty appendices epiploicae, and sacculated haustra.

vis.alt: Abdominal inspection landmarks showing large bowel topographical distribution
vis.caption: Topographical course of the colon from right iliac fossa across abdomen to pelvic brim. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The **taeniae coli** are three narrow longitudinal ribbons formed by condensation of the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the colonic wall. Because these muscular bands are approximately twenty percent shorter than the underlying circular muscle and mucosal layers, they gather the colon into distinctive sacculated pouches called haustra.
steps.say: Taeniae coli are three ribbons formed by the outer longitudinal muscle layer. Because they are shorter than the bowel wall, they gather the colon into pouches called haustra.

rows: Most visible band; easily traced to appendix base
Guides vascular entry to transverse colon
Overlain by greater omentum on transverse colon

steps.tx: The three taeniae coli converge precisely at the base of the vermiform appendix on the posteromedial wall of the caecum. During difficult emergency appendicectomy where the appendix is obscured by inflammatory adhesions, tracing the **taenia libera** downwards provides an infallible anatomical guide leading directly to the appendiceal root.
steps.say: The three taeniae coli meet at the base of the vermiform appendix. In difficult surgery, tracing the anterior free taenia libera downward leads infallibly to the root of the appendix.

steps.tx: Small peritoneal pouches filled with adipose tissue that project from the serosal surface of the colon are **appendices epiploicae**. Most numerous along the transverse and sigmoid colons, torsion or acute thrombosis of an appendix epiploica causes epiploic appendagitis, presenting with acute focal abdominal pain that mimics diverticulitis.
steps.say: Small fat-filled peritoneal sacs projecting from the colon are appendices epiploicae. Torsion of these appendages causes epiploic appendagitis, mimicking acute diverticulitis or appendicitis.

left.title: Appendices Epiploicae
points: Absent on caecum, appendix, and rectum
Contain central end-artery from colonic wall

right.title: Diverticulosis
points: Acquired mucosal herniations through circular muscle
Penetrate at sites where vasa recta pierce wall
Prevalent in sigmoid colon under high pressure

steps.tx: The midgut-derived large intestine (caecum, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of transverse colon) is supplied by the **superior mesenteric artery** via ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches. The hindgut-derived distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, and sigmoid are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.
steps.say: The colon receives a dual arterial supply. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the caecum to mid-transverse colon, while the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal transverse to sigmoid colon.

rows: Left colic, sigmoid arteries, superior rectal
Connects all colic branches 1 cm from wall
Direct trunk connecting middle to left colic

steps.tx: Running parallel to the inner border of the entire large intestine is the continuous **marginal artery of Drummond**, formed by anastomosing loops between all colic branches of the SMA and IMA. Situated approximately one centimetre from the mesenteric border, it delivers vasa recta to the colonic wall.
steps.say: The marginal artery of Drummond forms a continuous arterial channel along the inner border of the colon. Positioned one centimeter from the wall, it links SMA and IMA branches.

vis.alt: Abdominal radiograph showing colonic haustral markings and watershed ischemic distribution
vis.caption: Colonic architecture illustrating vascular watershed zones vulnerable to hypoperfusion. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Regions situated at the terminal junctions of two independent arterial territories are designated **watershed areas**. The most critical colonic watershed zone is Griffiths point at the splenic flexure, where the terminal branches of the middle colic artery (SMA) meet the ascending branch of the left colic artery (IMA).
steps.say: Watershed zones sit at the borders of distinct arterial supplies. The prime watershed is Griffiths point at the splenic flexure, bridging middle colic branches from the SMA with left colic from the IMA.

left.title: Griffiths Point (Splenic Flexure)
points: Junction of SMA (middle colic) and IMA (left colic)
Marginal artery of Drummond is often tenuous or absent
Prime site of non-occlusive ischemic colitis
Presents with crampy pain and bloody diarrhea

right.title: Sudeck Point (Rectosigmoid Junction)
points: Junction of lowest sigmoid artery and superior rectal
Critical junction in distal sigmoid colon
Vulnerable to ischemia during low anterior resection
Mandates testing marginal pulse before anastomosis

steps.tx: During systemic hypotension, septic shock, or cardiac arrest, low-flow states selectively starve the splenic flexure, precipitating **ischemic colitis**. Contrast computed tomography and endoscopy demonstrate focal mucosal edema, ulcerations, and thumbprinting in the watershed territory, sparing the well-perfused rectum and ascending colon.
steps.say: Systemic hypotension starves watershed zones, triggering ischemic colitis at the splenic flexure. Colonoscopy reveals dusky mucosa, ulcerations, and thumbprinting in the ischemic segment.
